item.title: New rockets to lift nation's launch capacity
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11
A major Chinese space enterprise is developing two new carrier rocket models and plans to conduct their debut flights next year, according to a top company official. Speaking on Monday at a commercial space forum in Wuhan, Hubei province, Zha Xiongquan, chairman of Expace Technology, said the company is developing the Kuaizhou 6 and Kuaizhou 12 rockets to meet the country's rapidly growing demand for high-capacity launch vehicles. "Expace has been leveraging mature technologies and existing production capacity to develop the Kuaizhou 12 — a low-cost medium-lift rocket that uses both solid and liquid propellants. It will have a launch cost of less than 20,000 yuan ($3,000) per kilogram," Zha said. The Kuaizhou 12 is scheduled to make its debut flight and enter commercial service in 2027. Its introduction is expected to help China's space industry break the bottleneck in low-cost, large-scale launch capacity. Zha said the company is also accelerating development of the reusable Kuaizhou 6 liquid-fueled rocket, which is on track to complete its first orbital flight and first-stage recovery next year. According to Expace designers, the Kuaizhou 12 will be about 47 meters tall and have a fairing diameter of 5.2 meters. It will be capable of carrying 10 metric tons of payload to a typical low-Earth orbit. The Kuaizhou 6 will be much taller at 73 meters, and it will have a booster diameter of 4.5 meters. In a nonrecoverable mission, the rocket will be able to carry 18 tons of payload to a low-Earth orbit. For reusable flights, which involve recovery of the first-stage booster, it will be able to carry 14 tons to the same orbit. The Kuaizhou is China's leading solid-propellant rocket series, in contrast to the Long March family, which relies mainly on liquid propellants. To date, the two main Kuaizhou models — 1A and 11 — have completed 37 flights, deploying nearly 100 satellites into space. Zha said at the forum that the Kuaizhou 1A and Kuaizhou 11 are expected to carry out more than 50 launches over the next three years. "Through regular, high-frequency launch services, these rockets will further cement the country's global lead in space rapid-response capabilities and support national emergency-response requirements," he said. zhaolei@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: 'Skillcations' enrich holiday experiences
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11
Chen Cong had planned to spend her holidays in Jingdezhen, Jiangxi province, wandering between kiln sites and ceramic markets. Then it rained for days. Not keen on traipsing from one soggy kiln to the next under an umbrella, the office worker from Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, signed up for a five-day ceramic-making course instead. She had no idea this one decision would lead her to a new passion and a rethink of how she spends her money and holidays. For five days, her mornings were spent learning wheel-throwing, hand-building, underglaze painting and glazing. Afternoons were for free creation or for browsing glaze and clay shops with classmates, learning about slips, colored glazes and kiln transmutations, and observing how different clays fire. In the evenings, she wandered the local ceramic markets for inspiration. "Pottery takes time. It's not something you can experience in just a short hour," she said, adding that Jingdezhen's five-day course offered an immersive learning experience. "As the birthplace of ceramics, Jingdezhen has a very good learning environment, with plenty of public kilns, clay shops and a dazzling variety of glaze shops," Chen said. Chen returned to Hangzhou with several pieces she had made, some to keep and some to give as gifts to colleagues and friends. Having hands-on experience of turning a lump of clay into a fine piece of porcelain greatly reduced her desire to buy new things. "Now when something at home breaks, I think about whether I can fix it myself," Chen said. The Jingdezhen stay also helped her find her own hobby — underglaze painting. She took home underglaze pigments and bisque wares, onto which she copies Chinese paintings in her spare time. Recently she returned to Jingdezhen for a weekend to have them fired. Vacations centered around learning a skill while exploring a destination, or "skillcations", have become one of the biggest travel trends in the country. According to a report by lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu on the interest-driven travel trend, searches for experiential activities such as crafts, heritage sites and the outdoors grew 48 percent quarter-on-quarter as of September. Besides Jingdezhen, other cities have also become popular skillcation destinations: Dali in Yunnan province offers visitors the chance to learn the tie-dye craft of the Bai ethnic group; She county in Anhui province is where visitors can experience gold tracing and Huizhou inkstick manufacturing at local factories; and Suzhou in Jiangsu province is where people can learn Suzhou embroidery. "I was already doing skillcation before the word was invented," said Liu Yuxi, a 27-year-old from Shenzhen, Guangdong province, who learned surfing while vacationing in Hainan province, Muay Thai in Thailand and diving in Vietnam. "Learning a new skill while on vacation is a way to enrich my travel experience," she said. She often travels to foreign countries, where she meets peers from various countries in youth hostels, many of whom have a skill to show off. "I even met a Spanish man who could perform Wing Chun moves and forms," Liu said, referring to a southern Chinese kung fu style. That inspired her to learn a skill that represented her own culture. Last year, she traveled to Foshan, Guangdong, to learn Wing Chun. After studying for a while, she realized that learning the traditional martial art was a dry and slow process. "It's something you should never expect to master quickly," she said. Liu found the repetitive daily practice of polishing forms similar to "inner observation", which gradually freed her from restlessness and made her more grounded. She has now been in Foshan for more than a year, and sometimes, because of her good English, she teaches trial classes to foreign tourists. "I've found that this is no longer just a hobby, but something I want to learn long-term and pass on," she said. She records her daily martial arts practice on video, edits it into vlogs and posts them on social media. "Now newcomers at the gym say they became interested in Wing Chun because they saw my videos," she said. Liu has bought a lifetime membership card for 8,000 yuan ($1,200) at a local Wing Chun gym in Foshan. "Now I plan to have the longest skillcation of my life in Foshan," she said.

item.title: Shanghai import expo sets several records
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11
Multiple records and trading vibrancy witnessed at the just-concluded 9th China International Import Expo in Shanghai mirror China's continued efforts to advance innovation and stabilize global trade to offset various headwinds, said experts and company executives. The value of intended deals reached at the expo rose 2.3 percent year-on-year to hit a record $85.45 billion, Xiao Lu, deputy Party secretary of the CIIE bureau, said at a news briefing on Tuesday, at the closing of the six-day event. Up to 485 new products, technologies and service items made their debut at this year's CIIE, up from 461 last year to reach a new high, Xiao said. Michael Jiang, head of Clients and Markets at KPMG China, said that the size and capacity of this year's CIIE has further demonstrated the demand potential and innovation vitality of the massive Chinese market, and companies discover more opportunities via the expo. Chinese and foreign firms alike can expand their cooperation by efficiently matching their demand, deepening industry coordination, seeking technology innovation and upgrading, as well as rebuilding the supply chain via the annual event, Jiang said. The expo reflects China's leading position in platform-driven trade, which has fundamentally changed the trajectory of global trade, transitioning from the domination of supply to demand, said Chen Wenling, senior researcher at the China Center for International Economic Exchanges (CCIEE). "China is like a tailor, stitching together the fractures in global trade, one stitch at a time," Chen said. The CIIE has also facilitated the upgrading and transformation of the Chinese economy at the demand end via the expo's high-quality, diversified and personalized product supply, added Chen. Patrik Ziman, CFO of Boehringer Ingelheim for Greater China, said the German company has introduced about 50 innovative products into China by participating in eight editions of the expo. Presence at the CIIE has helped the company conduct deeper exchanges with local governments, medical service providers, research institutes and industry partners. This has deepened the company's better understanding of the Chinese market and its integration of the Chinese innovative ecosystem, Ziman said. The expo itself has evolved from a trading platform to an international incubator, said Chen of the CCIEE. The demonstration of quantum technology, bio-manufacturing, hydrogen and nuclear fusion is in line with China's development goals in future-oriented industries. Advanced technologies both from home and abroad are connected and applied in real-case scenarios more efficiently, she said. The innovation incubation special section at this year's CIIE saw unprecedented participation by displaying 633 startup projects from nearly 40 countries and regions, up 20 percent from last year. "The CIIE has been repeating one truth: China is not only where global innovation can be applied, but also jointly created," said Mark Wang, president and CEO of HSBC China.

item.title: Data centers crank up job seekers' options
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11
With a flashlight, a set of keys, a two-way radio and an electrical meter in his backpack, shift leader Chen Gang made his rounds through the power distribution rooms and cooling areas of a massive data center in Ulaanqab, Inner Mongolia autonomous region. The facility, built and operated by GDS Holdings, hosts computing infrastructure for clients running heavy workloads including big-data batch processing, cloud storage and artificial intelligence. Chen checked instrument readings and indicator lights and made sure that switches were all in the right positions. As part of his duties, he also helps coordinate routine inspections and responses to equipment problems. His job is radically different from his last one serving guests at a hotel. Ulaanqab, once mainly known for potato farming, began developing its data processing industry more than a decade ago. It started with a strategic cooperation agreement on cloud computing with electronics giant Huawei in 2013. The Huawei Cloud Computing Data Center opened three years later. The city's cool climate, abundant wind and solar resources, and high-speed network connections to Beijing made it an ideal location for further data center investment. High-tech development gained further impetus in 2022, when the "East Data, West Computing" initiative was launched. The project aims to coordinate the computing capabilities of the country's eastern regions, where the need for computing is high, with inland western regions, where abundant renewable resources are optimal for the construction of data centers. Ulaanqab has since become a key location in the Inner Mongolian hub of an integrated national network. As of October, the city had signed agreements for 109 computing center projects. It reported an operating capacity of 190,000 PFLOPS — a measure of computer processing speed that equals 1 quadrillion floating-point operations per second and an indicator of how fast a computer can do heavy, precision math calculations.

item.title: China transfers US pilots' remains
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
The Chinese military handed over the remains of United States pilots, who aided China during the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) to the US military, in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province, on Tuesday. The remains of the US pilots, which were transferred by China to the US, had recently been recovered from areas along the Hump Route, a vital World War II aerial supply line. The handover ceremony, which was held at the Jianchuan Museum Cluster in Chengdu, was attended by representatives of the Chinese and US militaries, and local officials. A senior official from the Archives Bureau of the General Office of the Central Military Commission said that the handover reflects the history of Chinese and US forces fighting side by side against Japanese aggression during World War II. The official said that Tuesday's ceremony "helps to bring these fallen heroes home and commemorates the long-standing friendship between China and the US, forged through shared hardships". An official from the US Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency said that the handover was the culmination of years of sustained joint efforts, adding that it was a deeply meaningful event. The US official said that the remains represent a defining moment in history when Americans, driven by a sense of duty to resist aggression, stood alongside the Chinese people to fight a common threat. The remains were discovered along the Hump Route, an air corridor that crossed the Himalayas into Sichuan. The route served as a supply lifeline for China from 1942 to 1945, supporting the country's resistance against Japanese aggression. The American Volunteer Group of the Chinese Air Force, better known as the Flying Tigers, played a key role in opening and protecting the route during World War II. More than 1,700 Chinese and US aircrew members lost their lives along this vital corridor, making the Hump Route a testament to the two countries' joint efforts during the war, according to historical records. Since the defense ministries of the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in 2008 on military archive cooperation, bilateral cooperation in this field has continued uninterrupted. Both sides have engaged in friendly, practical and effective cooperation based on the principles of equality through consultation, mutual benefit and reciprocity, the Chinese authorities said. Over the past 18 years, search and excavation teams have conducted field investigations in more than 100 locations across China. In addition, a growing number of volunteers have participated in the search efforts. Fan Jianchuan, director of the Jianchuan Museum Cluster, said that the institution raised funds and assembled a professional team that conducted several expeditions into uninhabited and glacier-covered areas to search for the wreckage of US aircraft that aided China during World War II. Fan said that the team recovered eight bone fragments during its latest expedition. "The Chinese nation values gratitude and reciprocity, and we hope that the friendship forged between China and the US during the World Anti-Fascist War will endure," he added. In April last year, China handed over the remains of US pilots found in Hengdong county, Hunan province. An earlier handover of such remains took place at the Jianchuan Museum Cluster in October 2015. China is willing to continue practical cooperation with the US in this field and contribute positively to building a constructive relationship of strategic stability between the two countries, the Ministry of National Defense said. lishangyi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Momentum in trade bolsters growth outlook
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
China's foreign trade growth, building on a steady climb up the export value chain and a massive domestic market that is opening wider to imports, is delivering a crucial boost to economic growth in the final stretch of the year, experts and executives said. The country's pursuit of more balanced foreign trade promises greater opportunities for global businesses, while reinforcing China's role as an anchor of stability for the world economy, they added. Their comments came as the General Administration of Customs said on Tuesday that the total value of China's goods imports and exports reached 44.81 trillion yuan ($6.7 trillion) in the first 10 months of 2026, up 20 percent year-on-year. Exports helped fuel overall trade growth, with shipments rising 17.6 percent year-on-year to 25.99 trillion yuan over the period. Exports of mechanical and electrical products grew at a faster pace, up 25.2 percent year-on-year to 16.81 trillion yuan. Behind much of China's export strength this year is the global boom in artificial intelligence investment, which has provided a growing boost to shipments of chips and related products, said Feng Lin, executive director of research at Orient Golden Credit Rating International. "A steadily improving export mix is also becoming an important driver of export growth," she said, noting that years of manufacturing upgrades continue to bolster exports of high-tech goods. That industrial progress has gradually shifted China's manufacturing edge from low labor costs toward "a combination of strengths in supply chains, technological innovation and production efficiency", said Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities. Inside the workshops of Kyocera Document Technology (Dongguan) Co, an office equipment manufacturer in Guangdong province, a batch of newly developed multifunction printers awaits shipment to Southeast Asia, according to Huangpu Customs in Guangdong. Yuan Xiji, a company executive, explained how the company climbs up the value chain. "We used to focus on basic assembly and processing, but have since become a research and development center." Luo, the economist, said the gains from exports also feed through to the wider economy, as stronger demand brings more orders to manufacturers, spurs production and helps underpin the recovery. Foreign trade's contribution to growth is reflected in data from the National Bureau of Statistics, which showed that net exports of goods and services added 1.2 percentage points to GDP growth in the first three quarters. Exports also generate substantial investment and consumption, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs. Meanwhile, robust import growth is also emerging as a stabilizing force, as the rapid expansion of high-tech industries fuels demand in the domestic market. According to the General Administration of Customs, total goods imports grew 23.6 percent year-on-year to 18.82 trillion yuan in the first 10 months, with the value of integrated circuit imports surging 58 percent. In October alone, total imports climbed 34.7 percent year-on-year to 2.08 trillion yuan. "We expect imports in US dollar terms to maintain strong year-on-year growth of around 30 percent in November," said Feng of Orient Golden Credit Rating International. The upbeat outlook comes as the world's second-largest importer seeks to promote "balanced development of imports and exports", a goal set out in China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30). "The Chinese market is an anchor of resilience for the global economy," said Wang Xuekun, head of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation. Beyond its vast market, China is also encouraging open innovation, with its technological advances providing fresh impetus for global development, Wang said. Xiao Ping, the China and Asia regional hub manager for IEC LV Motors at ABB Group's motion business, said, "China's industrial capabilities and supply chain advantages are irreplaceable." The Swiss company sees considerable opportunities for energy-efficient cooling systems in China and overseas markets as AI drives growing demand for computing infrastructure worldwide, Xiao said.

item.title: Hangzhou across 5,000 years: From ancient Liangzhu to the future
item.description:

More than 5,000 years ago, Liangzhu was home to rice cultivation. Besides vast water management system and intricate jade artifacts, the planned city is a testimony to the existence of Chinese civilization at least 5,000 years ago. Today, experts from around the world gathered in Hangzhou to discuss heritage conservation and facilitate mutual learning among civilizations. Join China Daily's digital employee Yuanxi and cultural heritage vlogger Dong Zhen on a journey from ancient Liangzhu to modern Hangzhou.

item.title: Xi's Vision: Why Shenzhen?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10
Xi's Vision: Why Shenzhen?
By Luo Yueya, Du Wenjuan, Song Wei, Xu Wei, Qin Jize, and Zhang Chunyan | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-11-10 10:58
Share - WeChat
In December 2012, Xi Jinping chose Shenzhen for his first local inspection tour as China's top leader, reaffirming the country's commitment to reform and opening-up, and calling for bold exploration and innovation. Today, Shenzhen attracts entrepreneurs, engineers and scientists from around the world. Why Shenzhen? China Daily host Dylan Walker visits the city to hear the stories of the people who helped build it, and entrepreneurs from around the world, exploring what continues to drive Shenzhen's remarkable capacity for innovation and growth.
